- Egg, chicken, ham, tuna, and macaroni salads can be stored in the refrigerator for 3 to 4 days. [4]

How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely (Food Standards Agency, 2017):
- Defrost food in the fridge using a container big enough to catch any drips and use it within 24 hours after it is fully defrosted. [1]
- If a fridge is not possible, defrost food in the microwave on the defrost setting directly before cooking. [1]

Kitchen Companion: Your Safe Food Handbook (U.S. Department of Agriculture, Food Safety and Inspection Service, 2015):
- Thaw meat and poultry safely in the refrigerator, placing it on a plate or in a pan to catch any juices. [4]
- For faster thawing, submerge a sealed frozen package in cold water, changing the water every 30 minutes, and cook immediately after thawing. [4]
- When using a microwave to thaw, follow the oven manufacturer’s instructions and cook the food immediately after thawing. [4]

From The Eatwell Guide (Public Health England, 2018):
- Adults should aim to drink 6-8 cups or glasses of fluid every day. [1]
- Aim to drink 6-8 glasses of fluid every day. [2]

The Eatwell Guide (Public Health England, 2018):
- Unsaturated oils such as vegetable oil, rapeseed oil and olive oil are healthier fats and swapping to them helps reduce blood cholesterol. [1]
- Choosing lower‑fat spreads instead of butter is a good way to reduce saturated fat intake. [1]
- All types of fat are high in energy and should be limited in the diet. [1]
- Use unsaturated oils and soft spreads made from unsaturated oils sparingly because they are high in fat. [5]
- Choose lower‑fat spreads where possible and select oils that are high in unsaturated fat and low in saturated fat. [5]
- Heating oil in the pan before use makes it expand, allowing you to use less oil. [5]

What are healthy diets? Joint statement by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations and the World Health Organization (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations and World Health Organization, 2024):
- WHO recommends replacing saturated fatty acids in the diet with polyunsaturated fatty acids (strong recommendation) and monounsaturated fatty acids from plant sources (conditional recommendation). [3]
- WHO recommends that adults and children reduce saturated fatty acid intake to 10% of total energy intake (strong recommendation). [3]

These documents each address this:

The Eatwell Guide (Public Health England, 2018):
- Ideally, no more than 5% of the energy we consume should come from free sugars. [1]
- From age 11 years and for adults, the recommended maximum free sugars intake is no more than 30 g per day (7 sugar cubes). [1]

Healthy diet (Fact sheet N°394) (World Health Organization, 2018):
- Both adults and children should reduce free sugars intake to less than 10% of total energy intake. [2]
- Reducing free sugars intake to less than 5% of total energy would provide additional health benefits. [2]
- Adults should limit free sugars to less than 10% of total energy intake, ideally less than 5% for extra benefits. [6]

Kitchen Companion: Your Safe Food Handbook (U.S. Department of Agriculture, Food Safety and Inspection Service, 2015):
- Keep hot food at 140 °F (60 °C) or above. [2]
- Keep cold food at 40 °F (4.44 °C) or below. [2]

How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely (Food Standards Agency, 2017):
- Set your fridge between 0 and 5 °C and use a fridge thermometer to check it weekly. [3]
- Do not place hot or warm food directly in the fridge; cool it at room temperature and refrigerate within one to two hours. [3]
- Eat refrigerated leftovers within 48 hours or freeze them. [3]
- Your freezer should be around –18 °C. [4]
- Keep chilled food out of the fridge for a maximum of four hours during preparation. [4]
- Eat leftovers within two days or freeze them if they will not be eaten within that time. [4]

From Kitchen Companion: Your Safe Food Handbook (U.S. Department of Agriculture, Food Safety and Inspection Service, 2015):
- Reheat leftovers to 165 °F (73.9 °C) and use a food thermometer to verify the temperature. [1]
- Reheat leftovers to at least 165 °F (73.9 °C), confirming with a food thermometer before consumption. [2]
- Reheat take‑out or delivered leftovers to 165 °F (73.9 °C) as you would any leftover. [3]

From Five Keys to Safer Food Manual (World Health Organization, 2006):
- Separating raw food from cooked food prevents cross‑contamination, which is the introduction of microorganisms from raw food into ready‑to‑eat food making it unsafe. [4]
- Keeping raw and cooked foods separate reduces the risk that microorganisms transferred by hands, cloths or utensils cause foodborne disease. [5]
